results.content:
1	From "Exploiting correlations across trials and behavioral sessions to improve neural decoding"
2	
3	Our goal is to decode behavior y \in R^P from spike-sorted, temporally binned spike counts. For each trial k, neural activity has size N x T, where N is the number of neurons and T the number of time steps. Recordings are split into 2-s trials, each divided into 20-ms bins, producing T = 100 time steps. For each trial, we constructed X \in R^{N x T}  by aggregating spike counts and used it to compute a decoder estimate of the true behavior y \in R^P. y is constant within a trial (“per-trial decoding”); when P = T, y varies across time (“per-timestep decoding”).
4	
5	We apply our models to 433 IBL sessions,17 covering 270 brain regions and four behavioral variables: choice, prior, wheel speed, and whisker motion energy.
6	
7	 In the IBL experiments, mice rotate a wheel to indicate the location of a visual stimulus, defined as their choice (Figure 1A). For the first 90 trials, the stimulus appears randomly on either side with equal probability; in subsequent trials, it appears predominantly on one side in blocks. Mice adapt their behavior to these changing probabilities, allowing estimation of each mouse’s trial-by-trial prior belief (prior) about stimulus location. Additionally, wheel speed and whisker motion energy near the whisker pad are recorded. Whisker motion energy is computed as the mean absolute difference between adjacent video frames within a bounding box anchored between nose tip and eye. Choice and prior are static within a trial, while wheel speed and whisker motion energy are time-varying signals sampled at 60 Hz. See STAR Methods sections “data processing” and “hyperparameter selection” for details.
8	
9	Data processing
10	
11	IBL trial-aligned dataset
12	
13	For choice, we align trials to the stimulus onset, considering neural activity from 0.5 s before to 1.5 s post-onset. For prior, we also align trials to the stimulus onset, including neural activity from 0.6 s to 0.1 s pre-onset. The prior represents the mice’s estimate of the stimulus side probability. We use the same decoding window as in the previous study,27 focusing on the period with minimal wheel movements. Within each trial, we segment neural activity into 50-ms non-overlapping time bins. For each time bin, we bin spike counts using all neurons, sorted by Kilosort 2.5,77 from each session. For dynamic behaviors (wheel speed and whisker motion energy), we select the first movement onset as the alignment event, and decode the behavior starting at the alignment event and ending at 1 s after the alignment event. The neural activity within each trial is binned into non-overlapping 20 ms bins. For each time bin, we similarly bin spike counts using all neurons from each session.
14	
15	IBL trial-unaligned dataset
16	
17	We focus only on wheel speed and whisker motion energy, as variables like choice and prior are only defined during experimental trials, which are periods when stimuli are presented and mice respond for rewards. Unlike the trial-aligned dataset, we do not align neural activity and behavior to a specific event onset. Instead, we segment the continuous Neuropixels recordings into 2-s snippets to construct the trial-unaligned dataset for each session. These snippets cover intervals both during and outside experimental trials, capturing the repetitive, structured behaviors within trials as well as the more spontaneous behaviors outside of trials.
18	
19	From "A brain-wide map of neural activity during complex behaviour"
20	
21	We trained 139 mice (94 male and 45 female) on the International Brain Laboratory (IBL) decision-making task (Fig. 1a,b). On each trial, a visual stimulus appeared to the left or right on a screen, and the mouse had to move it to the centre by turning a wheel with its front paws within 60 s (Fig. 1c). After an initial 90 unbiased trials, the prior probability for the stimulus to appear on the left or right side was constant over a block of trials at a ratio of 20:80% (right block) or 80:20% (left block). Blocks lasted for between 20 and 100 trials, which were drawn from a truncated geometric distribution (empirical mean of 51 trials). Block changes were not cued. Stimulus contrast was uniformly sampled from 5 possible values (100, 25, 12.5, 6.25 and 0%). The 0% contrast trials, when no stimulus was presented, were assigned to a left or right side following the probability distribution of the block. This allowed mice to perform above chance by incorporating this prior in their choices. Following a wheel turn, mice received positive feedback in the form of a water reward, or negative feedback in the form of a white-noise pulse and a 2-s time out. The next trial began after a delay, followed by a quiescence period during which the mice had to hold the wheel still.
22	
23	Recordings
24	
25	In these mice, we inserted 699 Neuropixels probes (see an example of one recording of three trials in Fig. 1i), following a grid that covered the left hemisphere of the forebrain and midbrain, which typically represent stimuli or actions on the contralateral side, and the right hemisphere of the cerebellum and hindbrain, which typically represent the ipsilateral side (Fig. 2a). Recordings were collected by 12 laboratories in Europe and the USA, with most recordings using 2 simultaneous probe insertions. To ensure reproducibility, one brain location was targeted in every mouse in every laboratory, as described elsewhere25. Only sessions with at least 400 trials were retained for further analyses. Data were uploaded to a central server, preprocessed and shared through a standardized interface. To perform spike sorting on the recordings, we used a version of Kilosort with custom additions. This process produced 621,733 units (including multineuron activity), averaging 889 per probe. To separate individual neurons from clusters of multineuron activity, we then applied stringent quality-control metrics (based on those described in ref. 15), which identified 75,708 well-isolated neurons, averaging 108 per probe.
26	
27	Methods
28	
29	n brief, at the beginning of each trial, the mouse was required to not move the wheel for a quiescence period of 400–700 ms. After the quiescence period, a visual stimulus (Gabor patch) appeared on either the left or right (±35° azimuth) of the screen, with a contrast randomly sampled from a predefined set (100, 25, 12.5, 6 or 0%). A 100-ms tone (5-kHz sine wave) was played at stimulus onset. Mice had 60 s to move the wheel and make a response. Stimuli were yoked to the rotation of the response wheel, such that a 1-mm movement of the wheel moved the stimulus by 4 visual degrees. A response was registered if the centre of the stimulus crossed the  ±35° azimuth line from its original position. If the mouse correctly moved the stimulus 35° to the centre of the screen, it immediately received a 3-μl reward; if it incorrectly moved the stimulus 35° away from the centre, it received a time out. If the mouse responded incorrectly or failed to reach either threshold within the 60-s window, a white-noise burst was played for 500 ms and the inter-trial interval was between 1 and 1.5 s. In trials for which the visual stimulus contrast was set to 0%, the mouse had to respond as for any other trial by turning the wheel in the correct direction (assigned according to the statistics of the prevailing block) to receive a reward, but the mouse was not able to perceive whether the stimulus was presented on the left or right side of the screen. The mouse also received feedback (noise burst or reward) on 0% contrast trials.
30	
31	Each session started with 90 trials in which the probability of a visual stimulus appearing on the left or right side was equal. Specifically, the 100%, 25%, 12.5% and 6% contrast trials were each presented 10 times on each side, and the 0% contrast was presented 10 times in total (that is, the ratio of the 100, 25, 12.5, 6 and 0% contrasts were set at 2, 2, 2, 2 and 1, respectively). The side (and thus correct movement) for the 0% contrast trials was chosen randomly between the right and left with equal probability. This initial block of 90 trials is referred to as the unbiased block (50:50).
32	
33	After the unbiased block, trials were presented in biased blocks: in right-bias blocks, stimuli appeared on the right on 80% of the trials, whereas in left-bias blocks, stimuli appeared on the right on 20% of the trials. The ratio of the contrasts remained as above (2:2:2:2:1). Whether the first biased block in a session was left or right was randomly chosen, and blocks were then alternated. The length of a block was drawn from an exponential distribution with scale parameter of 60 trials, but truncated to lie between 20 and 100 trials.
34	
35	The automated shaping protocol for training involved two collections of sessions. In the first session, the animals started performing a version of the task without biased blocks and were then progressively introduced to harder stimuli with weaker contrasts as they became progressively more competent. They also experienced a debiasing protocol, which was intended to dissuade them from persisting with just one of the choices. Once they were performing sufficiently well on all non-zero contrasts, they were faced with the biased blocks. When, in turn, performance on those was adequate (including on 0% contrast trials, which are informed by the block), they graduated to recording. Supplementary Figure 8a shows a joint histogram of the number of sessions the mice took in the first and second collections (these were not correlated). Supplementary Figure 8b shows a joint histogram of the number of sessions the mice took in the second collection and the performance during the recording sessions. These were also not correlated.
36	
37	Inclusion criteria
38	
39	We applied a set of inclusion criteria to sessions, probes and neurons to ensure data quality. Supplementary Table 1 lists the consequences of these criteria for the number of sessions and probes that passed the criteria.
40	Sessions and insertions
41	
42	Each Neuropixels insertion was repeated in at least two laboratories, with reproducibility of outcomes across laboratories verified with extensive analyses that we have previously reported25.
43	
44	Sessions were included in the data release if the mice performed at least 250 trials, with a performance of at least 90% correct on 100% contrast trials for both left and right blocks, and, to be able to analyse the feedback variable, if there were at least 3 trials with incorrect choices (after applying the trial exclusions below). Furthermore, sessions were included in the release only if they reached threshold on a collection of hardware tests (definitions are available from GiHub (https://int-brain-lab.github.io/iblenv/_autosummary/ibllib.qc.task_metrics.html)).
45	
46	Insertions were excluded if the neural data failed the whole recording per visually assessed criteria of the ‘Recording Inclusion metrics and Guidelines for Optimal Reproducibility’ (RIGOR) from ref. 25, by presenting major artefacts (see examples in ref. 28) or if the probe tract could not be recovered during the histology procedure. Furthermore, only insertions for which alignments had been resolved (see appendix 6 of ref. 25 for definitions) were used in this study.
47	
48	After applying these criteria, a total of 459 sessions, 699 insertions and 621,733 neurons remained, constituting the publicly released dataset.
49	Trials
50	
51	For the analyses presented here, trials were excluded if one of the following trial events could not be detected: choice, probabilityLeft, feebackType, feeback times, stimON times and firstMovement times. Trials were further excluded if the time between stimulus onset and the first movement of the wheel (the first wheel-movement time) were outside the range of 0.08–2.00 s.
52	Neurons and brain regions
53	
54	Neurons generated by the spike-sorting pipeline were excluded from the analyses presented here if they failed one of the three criteria described in ref. 28 (the single unit computed metrics of RIGOR25): amplitude > 50 μV; noise cut-off < 20 μV; and refractory period violation. Neurons that passed these criteria were termed well-isolated neurons (or often just ‘neurons’) in this study. Out of the 621,733 units collected, 75,708 were considered well-isolated neurons. Final analyses were additionally restricted to regions that were designated grey matter in the adult mouse Allen Common Coordinate framework6, contained at least five well-isolated neurons per session and were recorded from in at least two such sessions.
55	
56	Video analysis
57	
58	We briefly describe the video analysis pipeline (full details can be found in ref. 105). The recording rigs contained three cameras: one called ‘left’ at full resolution (1,280 × 1,024) and 60 Hz, filming the mouse from one side; one called ‘right’, filming the mouse symmetrically from the other side at half resolution (640 × 512) and 150 Hz; and one called ‘body’ at half resolution and 30 Hz, filming the body of the mouse from above. We developed several quality-control metrics to detect raw video issues such as poor illumination (as infrared light bulbs broke) or accidental misplacement of the cameras105.
59	
60	We computed the motion energy (the mean across pixels of the absolute value of the difference between adjacent frames) of the whisker pad areas in the ‘left’ and ‘right’ videos (Fig. 1d). The whisker pad area was empirically defined using a rectangular bounding box anchored between the nose tip and the eye, both found using DeepLabCut106 (DLC; see more below). This metric quantifies motion in the whisker pad area and has a temporal resolution of the respective camera.
61	
62	We also performed markerless pose estimation of body parts using DLC31, which is used in a fully automated pipeline in IBL (v.2.1) to track various body parts such as the paws, nose, tongue and pupil (Fig. 1d). In all analyses using DLC estimates, we excluded predictions with likelihood < 0.9. Furthermore, we developed several quality-control metrics for the DLC traces105.
63	
64	Overview of decoding
65	
66	We performed a decoding analysis to measure how much information the activity of populations of neurons contained about task variables such as stimulus side and choice. To do this we, used cross-validated, maximum-likelihood regression with L1 regularization (to zero out the contribution from noisy neurons). The neural regressors were defined by binning the spike counts from each neuron in each session in a given region in a specific time window on each trial. The duration of the time window, the number of bins in that time window (that is, the bin size) and the trial event to which it was aligned depended on the variable that is the target of our regression (Supplementary Table 2). These factors are discussed further below and include a variety of behavioural and task variables: stimulus side, choice, feedback and wheel speed and velocity. Although a session may have included multiple probe insertions, we did not perform decoding on these probes separately because they are not independent. Instead, neurons in the same session and region were combined across probes for our decoding analysis. Decoding was cross-validated and compared with a null distribution to test for significance. A given region may have been recorded on multiple sessions; therefore, in the main figures (Figs. 4–7) the region P value was defined by combining session P values using Fisher’s combined probability test, and the region effect size was defined by subtracting the median of the null distribution from the decoding score and reporting the median of the resulting values across sessions. The P values for all regions were then subjected to FDR correction for multiple comparisons at q = 0.01.
67	
68	Decoding target variables
69	
70	Stimulus side, choice and feedback were treated as binary target variables for logistic regression. For stimulus side, trials that had zero contrast were excluded. We used the LogisticRegression module from scikit-learn111 (v.1.1.2) with 0.001 tolerance, 20,000 maximum iterations, “l1” penalty, “liblinear” solver and “fit_intercept” set to True. We balanced decoder classes by weighting samples by the inverse of the class frequency, 1/(2Pi,class). Decoding performance was evaluated using the balanced accuracy of classification, which is the average of the recall probabilities for the two classes. Supplementary Figure 9 shows histograms of the regression coefficients for all the variables.
71	
72	Wheel values (speed and velocity) change over the course of a trial, unlike the previous decoding targets, and we therefore had to treat these target variables differently. We averaged wheel values in nonoverlapping 20-ms bins, starting 200 ms before first wheel-movement time and ending at 1,000 ms after first wheel-movement time. Spike counts were similarly binned. The target value for a given bin (ending at time t) was decoded from spikes in a preceding (causal) window spanning W bins (ending at times t, …, t-W). Therefore, if decoding from n neurons, there were (W + 1)n predictors of the target variable in a given bin. In practice, we used W = 10. To decode these continuous-valued targets, we performed linear regression using the Lasso module from scikit-learn111 (v.1.1.2) with 0.001 tolerance, 1,000 maximum iterations and “fit_intercept” set to True. Decoding performance was evaluated using the R2 metric.
73

From "Exploiting correlations across trials and behavioral sessions to improve neural decoding"

Our goal is to decode behavior y \in R^P from spike-sorted, temporally binned spike counts. For each trial k, neural activity has size N x T, where N is the number of neurons and T the number of time steps. Recordings are split into 2-s trials, each divided into 20-ms bins, producing T = 100 time steps. For each trial, we constructed X \in R^{N x T}  by aggregating spike counts and used it to compute a decoder estimate of the true behavior y \in R^P. y is constant within a trial (“per-trial decoding”); when P = T, y varies across time (“per-timestep decoding”).

We apply our models to 433 IBL sessions,17 covering 270 brain regions and four behavioral variables: choice, prior, wheel speed, and whisker motion energy.

 In the IBL experiments, mice rotate a wheel to indicate the location of a visual stimulus, defined as their choice (Figure 1A). For the first 90 trials, the stimulus appears randomly on either side with equal probability; in subsequent trials, it appears predominantly on one side in blocks. Mice adapt their behavior to these changing probabilities, allowing estimation of each mouse’s trial-by-trial prior belief (prior) about stimulus location. Additionally, wheel speed and whisker motion energy near the whisker pad are recorded. Whisker motion energy is computed as the mean absolute difference between adjacent video frames within a bounding box anchored between nose tip and eye. Choice and prior are static within a trial, while wheel speed and whisker motion energy are time-varying signals sampled at 60 Hz. See STAR Methods sections “data processing” and “hyperparameter selection” for details.

Data processing

IBL trial-aligned dataset

For choice, we align trials to the stimulus onset, considering neural activity from 0.5 s before to 1.5 s post-onset. For prior, we also align trials to the stimulus onset, including neural activity from 0.6 s to 0.1 s pre-onset. The prior represents the mice’s estimate of the stimulus side probability. We use the same decoding window as in the previous study,27 focusing on the period with minimal wheel movements. Within each trial, we segment neural activity into 50-ms non-overlapping time bins. For each time bin, we bin spike counts using all neurons, sorted by Kilosort 2.5,77 from each session. For dynamic behaviors (wheel speed and whisker motion energy), we select the first movement onset as the alignment event, and decode the behavior starting at the alignment event and ending at 1 s after the alignment event. The neural activity within each trial is binned into non-overlapping 20 ms bins. For each time bin, we similarly bin spike counts using all neurons from each session.

IBL trial-unaligned dataset

We focus only on wheel speed and whisker motion energy, as variables like choice and prior are only defined during experimental trials, which are periods when stimuli are presented and mice respond for rewards. Unlike the trial-aligned dataset, we do not align neural activity and behavior to a specific event onset. Instead, we segment the continuous Neuropixels recordings into 2-s snippets to construct the trial-unaligned dataset for each session. These snippets cover intervals both during and outside experimental trials, capturing the repetitive, structured behaviors within trials as well as the more spontaneous behaviors outside of trials.

In these mice, we inserted 699 Neuropixels probes (see an example of one recording of three trials in Fig. 1i), following a grid that covered the left hemisphere of the forebrain and midbrain, which typically represent stimuli or actions on the contralateral side, and the right hemisphere of the cerebellum and hindbrain, which typically represent the ipsilateral side (Fig. 2a). To separate individual neurons from clusters of multineuron activity, we then applied stringent quality-control metrics (based on those described in ref. 15), which identified 75,708 well-isolated neurons, averaging 108 per probe.

Methods

n brief, at the beginning of each trial, the mouse was required to not move the wheel for a quiescence period of 400–700 ms. If the mouse correctly moved the stimulus 35° to the centre of the screen, it immediately received a 3-μl reward; if it incorrectly moved the stimulus 35° away from the centre, it received a time out. In trials for which the visual stimulus contrast was set to 0%, the mouse had to respond as for any other trial by turning the wheel in the correct direction (assigned according to the statistics of the prevailing block) to receive a reward, but the mouse was not able to perceive whether the stimulus was presented on the left or right side of the screen. The mouse also received feedback (noise burst or reward) on 0% contrast trials.

Each session started with 90 trials in which the probability of a visual stimulus appearing on the left or right side was equal. Specifically, the 100%, 25%, 12.5% and 6% contrast trials were each presented 10 times on each side, and the 0% contrast was presented 10 times in total (that is, the ratio of the 100, 25, 12.5, 6 and 0% contrasts were set at 2, 2, 2, 2 and 1, respectively). The side (and thus correct movement) for the 0% contrast trials was chosen randomly between the right and left with equal probability. This initial block of 90 trials is referred to as the unbiased block (50:50).

After the unbiased block, trials were presented in biased blocks: in right-bias blocks, stimuli appeared on the right on 80% of the trials, whereas in left-bias blocks, stimuli appeared on the right on 20% of the trials. The ratio of the contrasts remained as above (2:2:2:2:1). Whether the first biased block in a session was left or right was randomly chosen, and blocks were then alternated. The length of a block was drawn from an exponential distribution with scale parameter of 60 trials, but truncated to lie between 20 and 100 trials.

The automated shaping protocol for training involved two collections of sessions. In the first session, the animals started performing a version of the task without biased blocks and were then progressively introduced to harder stimuli with weaker contrasts as they became progressively more competent. They also experienced a debiasing protocol, which was intended to dissuade them from persisting with just one of the choices. Once they were performing sufficiently well on all non-zero contrasts, they were faced with the biased blocks. When, in turn, performance on those was adequate (including on 0% contrast trials, which are informed by the block), they graduated to recording. Supplementary Figure 8a shows a joint histogram of the number of sessions the mice took in the first and second collections (these were not correlated). Supplementary Figure 8b shows a joint histogram of the number of sessions the mice took in the second collection and the performance during the recording sessions. These were also not correlated.

Inclusion criteria

We applied a set of inclusion criteria to sessions, probes and neurons to ensure data quality. Supplementary Table 1 lists the consequences of these criteria for the number of sessions and probes that passed the criteria.
Sessions and insertions

Each Neuropixels insertion was repeated in at least two laboratories, with reproducibility of outcomes across laboratories verified with extensive analyses that we have previously reported25.

Sessions were included in the data release if the mice performed at least 250 trials, with a performance of at least 90% correct on 100% contrast trials for both left and right blocks, and, to be able to analyse the feedback variable, if there were at least 3 trials with incorrect choices (after applying the trial exclusions below). Furthermore, sessions were included in the release only if they reached threshold on a collection of hardware tests (definitions are available from GiHub (https://int-brain-lab.github.io/iblenv/_autosummary/ibllib.qc.task_metrics.html)).

Insertions were excluded if the neural data failed the whole recording per visually assessed criteria of the ‘Recording Inclusion metrics and Guidelines for Optimal Reproducibility’ (RIGOR) from ref. 25, by presenting major artefacts (see examples in ref. 28) or if the probe tract could not be recovered during the histology procedure. Furthermore, only insertions for which alignments had been resolved (see appendix 6 of ref. 25 for definitions) were used in this study.

After applying these criteria, a total of 459 sessions, 699 insertions and 621,733 neurons remained, constituting the publicly released dataset.
Trials

For the analyses presented here, trials were excluded if one of the following trial events could not be detected: choice, probabilityLeft, feebackType, feeback times, stimON times and firstMovement times. Trials were further excluded if the time between stimulus onset and the first movement of the wheel (the first wheel-movement time) were outside the range of 0.08–2.00 s.
Neurons and brain regions

Neurons generated by the spike-sorting pipeline were excluded from the analyses presented here if they failed one of the three criteria described in ref. 28 (the single unit computed metrics of RIGOR25): amplitude > 50 μV; noise cut-off < 20 μV; and refractory period violation. Neurons that passed these criteria were termed well-isolated neurons (or often just ‘neurons’) in this study. Out of the 621,733 units collected, 75,708 were considered well-isolated neurons. Final analyses were additionally restricted to regions that were designated grey matter in the adult mouse Allen Common Coordinate framework6, contained at least five well-isolated neurons per session and were recorded from in at least two such sessions.

Video analysis

We briefly describe the video analysis pipeline (full details can be found in ref. 105). The recording rigs contained three cameras: one called ‘left’ at full resolution (1,280 × 1,024) and 60 Hz, filming the mouse from one side; one called ‘right’, filming the mouse symmetrically from the other side at half resolution (640 × 512) and 150 Hz; and one called ‘body’ at half resolution and 30 Hz, filming the body of the mouse from above. We developed several quality-control metrics to detect raw video issues such as poor illumination (as infrared light bulbs broke) or accidental misplacement of the cameras105.

We computed the motion energy (the mean across pixels of the absolute value of the difference between adjacent frames) of the whisker pad areas in the ‘left’ and ‘right’ videos (Fig. 1d). The whisker pad area was empirically defined using a rectangular bounding box anchored between the nose tip and the eye, both found using DeepLabCut106 (DLC; see more below). This metric quantifies motion in the whisker pad area and has a temporal resolution of the respective camera.

We also performed markerless pose estimation of body parts using DLC31, which is used in a fully automated pipeline in IBL (v.2.1) to track various body parts such as the paws, nose, tongue and pupil (Fig. 1d). In all analyses using DLC estimates, we excluded predictions with likelihood < 0.9. Furthermore, we developed several quality-control metrics for the DLC traces105.

Overview of decoding

We performed a decoding analysis to measure how much information the activity of populations of neurons contained about task variables such as stimulus side and choice. To do this we, used cross-validated, maximum-likelihood regression with L1 regularization (to zero out the contribution from noisy neurons). The neural regressors were defined by binning the spike counts from each neuron in each session in a given region in a specific time window on each trial. The duration of the time window, the number of bins in that time window (that is, the bin size) and the trial event to which it was aligned depended on the variable that is the target of our regression (Supplementary Table 2). These factors are discussed further below and include a variety of behavioural and task variables: stimulus side, choice, feedback and wheel speed and velocity. Although a session may have included multiple probe insertions, we did not perform decoding on these probes separately because they are not independent. Instead, neurons in the same session and region were combined across probes for our decoding analysis. Decoding was cross-validated and compared with a null distribution to test for significance. A given region may have been recorded on multiple sessions; therefore, in the main figures (Figs. 4–7) the region P value was defined by combining session P values using Fisher’s combined probability test, and the region effect size was defined by subtracting the median of the null distribution from the decoding score and reporting the median of the resulting values across sessions. The P values for all regions were then subjected to FDR correction for multiple comparisons at q = 0.01.

Decoding target variables

Stimulus side, choice and feedback were treated as binary target variables for logistic regression. For stimulus side, trials that had zero contrast were excluded. We used the LogisticRegression module from scikit-learn111 (v.1.1.2) with 0.001 tolerance, 20,000 maximum iterations, “l1” penalty, “liblinear” solver and “fit_intercept” set to True. We balanced decoder classes by weighting samples by the inverse of the class frequency, 1/(2Pi,class). Decoding performance was evaluated using the balanced accuracy of classification, which is the average of the recall probabilities for the two classes. Supplementary Figure 9 shows histograms of the regression coefficients for all the variables.

Wheel values (speed and velocity) change over the course of a trial, unlike the previous decoding targets, and we therefore had to treat these target variables differently. We averaged wheel values in nonoverlapping 20-ms bins, starting 200 ms before first wheel-movement time and ending at 1,000 ms after first wheel-movement time. Spike counts were similarly binned. The target value for a given bin (ending at time t) was decoded from spikes in a preceding (causal) window spanning W bins (ending at times t, …, t-W). Therefore, if decoding from n neurons, there were (W + 1)n predictors of the target variable in a given bin. In practice, we used W = 10. To decode these continuous-valued targets, we performed linear regression using the Lasso module from scikit-learn111 (v.1.1.2) with 0.001 tolerance, 1,000 maximum iterations and “fit_intercept” set to True. Decoding performance was evaluated using the R2 metric.

Our goal is to decode behavior y \in R^P from spike-sorted, temporally binned spike counts. For each trial k, neural activity has size N x T, where N is the number of neurons and T the number of time steps. Recordings are split into 2-s trials, each divided into 20-ms bins, producing T = 100 time steps. For each trial, we constructed X \in R^{N x T}  by aggregating spike counts and used it to compute a decoder estimate of the true behavior y \in R^P. y is constant within a trial (“per-trial decoding”); when P = T, y varies across time (“per-timestep decoding”).

We use the same decoding window as in the previous study,27 focusing on the period with minimal wheel movements. Within each trial, we segment neural activity into 50-ms non-overlapping time bins. For each time bin, we bin spike counts using all neurons, sorted by Kilosort 2.5,77 from each session. For dynamic behaviors (wheel speed and whisker motion energy), we select the first movement onset as the alignment event, and decode the behavior starting at the alignment event and ending at 1 s after the alignment event. The neural activity within each trial is binned into non-overlapping 20 ms bins. For each time bin, we similarly bin spike counts using all neurons from each session.
14	
15	IBL trial-unaligned dataset
16	
17	We focus only on wheel speed and whisker motion energy, as variables like choice and prior are only defined during experimental trials, which are periods when stimuli are presented and mice respond for rewards. Unlike the trial-aligned dataset, we do not align neural activity and behavior to a specific event onset. Instead, we segment the continuous Neuropixels recordings into 2-s snippets to construct the trial-unaligned dataset for each session. These snippets cover intervals both during and outside experimental trials, capturing the repetitive, structured behaviors within trials as well as the more spontaneous behaviors outside of trials.
18	
19	From "A brain-wide map of neural activity during complex behaviour"
20	
21	We trained 139 mice (94 male and 45 female) on the International Brain Laboratory (IBL) decision-making task (Fig. 1a,b). On each trial, a visual stimulus appeared to the left or right on a screen, and the mouse had to move it to the centre by turning a wheel with its front paws within 60 s (Fig. 1c). After an initial 90 unbiased trials, the prior probability for the stimulus to appear on the left or right side was constant over a block of trials at a ratio of 20:80% (right block) or 80:20% (left block). Blocks lasted for between 20 and 100 trials, which were drawn from a truncated geometric distribution (empirical mean of 51 trials). Block changes were not cued. Stimulus contrast was uniformly sampled from 5 possible values (100, 25, 12.5, 6.25 and 0%). The 0% contrast trials, when no stimulus was presented, were assigned to a left or right side following the probability distribution of the block. This allowed mice to perform above chance by incorporating this prior in their choices. Following a wheel turn, mice received positive feedback in the form of a water reward, or negative feedback in the form of a white-noise pulse and a 2-s time out. The next trial began after a delay, followed by a quiescence period during which the mice had to hold the wheel still.
22	
23	Recordings
24	
25	In these mice, we inserted 699 Neuropixels probes (see an example of one recording of three trials in Fig. 1i), following a grid that covered the left hemisphere of the forebrain and midbrain, which typically represent stimuli or actions on the contralateral side, and the right hemisphere of the cerebellum and hindbrain, which typically represent the ipsilateral side (Fig. 2a). Recordings were collected by 12 laboratories in Europe and the USA, with most recordings using 2 simultaneous probe insertions. To ensure reproducibility, one brain location was targeted in every mouse in every laboratory, as described elsewhere25. Only sessions with at least 400 trials were retained for further analyses. Data were uploaded to a central server, preprocessed and shared through a standardized interface. To perform spike sorting on the recordings, we used a version of Kilosort with custom additions. This process produced 621,733 units (including multineuron activity), averaging 889 per probe. To separate individual neurons from clusters of multineuron activity, we then applied stringent quality-control metrics (based on those described in ref. 15), which identified 75,708 well-isolated neurons, averaging 108 per probe.
26	
27	Methods
28	
29	n brief, at the beginning of each trial, the mouse was required to not move the wheel for a quiescence period of 400–700 ms. After the quiescence period, a visual stimulus (Gabor patch) appeared on either the left or right (±35° azimuth) of the screen, with a contrast randomly sampled from a predefined set (100, 25, 12.5, 6 or 0%). A 100-ms tone (5-kHz sine wave) was played at stimulus onset. Mice had 60 s to move the wheel and make a response. Stimuli were yoked to the rotation of the response wheel, such that a 1-mm movement of the wheel moved the stimulus by 4 visual degrees. A response was registered if the centre of the stimulus crossed the  ±35° azimuth line from its original position. If the mouse correctly moved the stimulus 35° to the centre of the screen, it immediately received a 3-μl reward; if it incorrectly moved the stimulus 35° away from the centre, it received a time out. If the mouse responded incorrectly or failed to reach either threshold within the 60-s window, a white-noise burst was played for 500 ms and the inter-trial interval was between 1 and 1.5 s. In trials for which the visual stimulus contrast was set to 0%, the mouse had to respond as for any other trial by turning the wheel in the correct direction (assigned according to the statistics of the prevailing block) to receive a reward, but the mouse was not able to perceive whether the stimulus was presented on the left or right side of the screen. The mouse also received feedback (noise burst or reward) on 0% contrast trials.
30	
31	Each session started with 90 trials in which the probability of a visual stimulus appearing on the left or right side was equal. Specifically, the 100%, 25%, 12.5% and 6% contrast trials were each presented 10 times on each side, and the 0% contrast was presented 10 times in total (that is, the ratio of the 100, 25, 12.5, 6 and 0% contrasts were set at 2, 2, 2, 2 and 1, respectively). The side (and thus correct movement) for the 0% contrast trials was chosen randomly between the right and left with equal probability. This initial block of 90 trials is referred to as the unbiased block (50:50).
32	
33	After the unbiased block, trials were presented in biased blocks: in right-bias blocks, stimuli appeared on the right on 80% of the trials, whereas in left-bias blocks, stimuli appeared on the right on 20% of the trials. The ratio of the contrasts remained as above (2:2:2:2:1). Whether the first biased block in a session was left or right was randomly chosen, and blocks were then alternated. The length of a block was drawn from an exponential distribution with scale parameter of 60 trials, but truncated to lie between 20 and 100 trials.
34	
35	The automated shaping protocol for training involved two collections of sessions. In the first session, the animals started performing a version of the task without biased blocks and were then progressively introduced to harder stimuli with weaker contrasts as they became progressively more competent. They also experienced a debiasing protocol, which was intended to dissuade them from persisting with just one of the choices. Once they were performing sufficiently well on all non-zero contrasts, they were faced with the biased blocks. When, in turn, performance on those was adequate (including on 0% contrast trials, which are informed by the block), they graduated to recording. Supplementary Figure 8a shows a joint histogram of the number of sessions the mice took in the first and second collections (these were not correlated). Supplementary Figure 8b shows a joint histogram of the number of sessions the mice took in the second collection and the performance during the recording sessions. These were also not correlated.
36	
37	Inclusion criteria
38	
39	We applied a set of inclusion criteria to sessions, probes and neurons to ensure data quality. Supplementary Table 1 lists the consequences of these criteria for the number of sessions and probes that passed the criteria.
40	Sessions and insertions
41	
42	Each Neuropixels insertion was repeated in at least two laboratories, with reproducibility of outcomes across laboratories verified with extensive analyses that we have previously reported25.
43	
44	Sessions were included in the data release if the mice performed at least 250 trials, with a performance of at least 90% correct on 100% contrast trials for both left and right blocks, and, to be able to analyse the feedback variable, if there were at least 3 trials with incorrect choices (after applying the trial exclusions below). Furthermore, sessions were included in the release only if they reached threshold on a collection of hardware tests (definitions are available from GiHub (https://int-brain-lab.github.io/iblenv/_autosummary/ibllib.qc.task_metrics.html)).
45	
46	Insertions were excluded if the neural data failed the whole recording per visually assessed criteria of the ‘Recording Inclusion metrics and Guidelines for Optimal Reproducibility’ (RIGOR) from ref. 25, by presenting major artefacts (see examples in ref. 28) or if the probe tract could not be recovered during the histology procedure. Furthermore, only insertions for which alignments had been resolved (see appendix 6 of ref. 25 for definitions) were used in this study.
47	
48	After applying these criteria, a total of 459 sessions, 699 insertions and 621,733 neurons remained, constituting the publicly released dataset.
49	Trials
50	
51	For the analyses presented here, trials were excluded if one of the following trial events could not be detected: choice, probabilityLeft, feebackType, feeback times, stimON times and firstMovement times. Trials were further excluded if the time between stimulus onset and the first movement of the wheel (the first wheel-movement time) were outside the range of 0.08–2.00 s.
52	Neurons and brain regions
53	
54	Neurons generated by the spike-sorting pipeline were excluded from the analyses presented here if they failed one of the three criteria described in ref. 28 (the single unit computed metrics of RIGOR25): amplitude > 50 μV; noise cut-off < 20 μV; and refractory period violation. Neurons that passed these criteria were termed well-isolated neurons (or often just ‘neurons’) in this study. Out of the 621,733 units collected, 75,708 were considered well-isolated neurons. Final analyses were additionally restricted to regions that were designated grey matter in the adult mouse Allen Common Coordinate framework6, contained at least five well-isolated neurons per session and were recorded from in at least two such sessions.
55	
56	Video analysis
57	
58	We briefly describe the video analysis pipeline (full details can be found in ref. 105). The recording rigs contained three cameras: one called ‘left’ at full resolution (1,280 × 1,024) and 60 Hz, filming the mouse from one side; one called ‘right’, filming the mouse symmetrically from the other side at half resolution (640 × 512) and 150 Hz; and one called ‘body’ at half resolution and 30 Hz, filming the body of the mouse from above. We developed several quality-control metrics to detect raw video issues such as poor illumination (as infrared light bulbs broke) or accidental misplacement of the cameras105.
59	
60	We computed the motion energy (the mean across pixels of the absolute value of the difference between adjacent frames) of the whisker pad areas in the ‘left’ and ‘right’ videos (Fig. 1d). The whisker pad area was empirically defined using a rectangular bounding box anchored between the nose tip and the eye, both found using DeepLabCut106 (DLC; see more below). This metric quantifies motion in the whisker pad area and has a temporal resolution of the respective camera.
61	
62	We also performed markerless pose estimation of body parts using DLC31, which is used in a fully automated pipeline in IBL (v.2.1) to track various body parts such as the paws, nose, tongue and pupil (Fig. 1d). In all analyses using DLC estimates, we excluded predictions with likelihood < 0.9. Furthermore, we developed several quality-control metrics for the DLC traces105.
63	
64	Overview of decoding
65	
66	We performed a decoding analysis to measure how much information the activity of populations of neurons contained about task variables such as stimulus side and choice. To do this we, used cross-validated, maximum-likelihood regression with L1 regularization (to zero out the contribution from noisy neurons). The neural regressors were defined by binning the spike counts from each neuron in each session in a given region in a specific time window on each trial. The duration of the time window, the number of bins in that time window (that is, the bin size) and the trial event to which it was aligned depended on the variable that is the target of our regression (Supplementary Table 2). These factors are discussed further below and include a variety of behavioural and task variables: stimulus side, choice, feedback and wheel speed and velocity. Although a session may have included multiple probe insertions, we did not perform decoding on these probes separately because they are not independent. Instead, neurons in the same session and region were combined across probes for our decoding analysis. Decoding was cross-validated and compared with a null distribution to test for significance. A given region may have been recorded on multiple sessions; therefore, in the main figures (Figs. 4–7) the region P value was defined by combining session P values using Fisher’s combined probability test, and the region effect size was defined by subtracting the median of the null distribution from the decoding score and reporting the median of the resulting values across sessions. The P values for all regions were then subjected to FDR correction for multiple comparisons at q = 0.01.
67	
68	Decoding target variables
69	
70	Stimulus side, choice and feedback were treated as binary target variables for logistic regression. For stimulus side, trials that had zero contrast were excluded. We used the LogisticRegression module from scikit-learn111 (v.1.1.2) with 0.001 tolerance, 20,000 maximum iterations, “l1” penalty, “liblinear” solver and “fit_intercept” set to True. We balanced decoder classes by weighting samples by the inverse of the class frequency, 1/(2Pi,class). Decoding performance was evaluated using the balanced accuracy of classification, which is the average of the recall probabilities for the two classes. Supplementary Figure 9 shows histograms of the regression coefficients for all the variables.
71	
72	Wheel values (speed and velocity) change over the course of a trial, unlike the previous decoding targets, and we therefore had to treat these target variables differently. We averaged wheel values in nonoverlapping 20-ms bins, starting 200 ms before first wheel-movement time and ending at 1,000 ms after first wheel-movement time. Spike counts were similarly binned. The target value for a given bin (ending at time t) was decoded from spikes in a preceding (causal) window spanning W bins (ending at times t, …, t-W). Therefore, if decoding from n neurons, there were (W + 1)n predictors of the target variable in a given bin. In practice, we used W = 10. To decode these continuous-valued targets, we performed linear regression using the Lasso module from scikit-learn111 (v.1.1.2) with 0.001 tolerance, 1,000 maximum iterations and “fit_intercept” set to True. Decoding performance was evaluated using the R2 metric.

import os
import sys
import argparse
from pathlib import Path
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from one.api import ONE
from datasets import DatasetDict
from utils.ibl_data_utils import (
    prepare_data, 
    select_brain_regions, 
    list_brain_regions, 
    bin_spiking_data,
    bin_behaviors,
    align_spike_behavior
)
from utils.dataset_utils import create_dataset, upload_dataset

ap = argparse.ArgumentParser()
ap.add_argument("--base_path", type=str, default="EXAMPLE_PATH")
ap.add_argument("--datasets", type=str, default="reproducible-ephys", choices=["reproducible-ephys", "brain-wide-map"])
ap.add_argument("--n_sessions", type=int, default=1)
ap.add_argument("--n_workers", type=int, default=1)
args = ap.parse_args()

SEED = 42

np.random.seed(SEED)

one = ONE(
    base_url='https://openalyx.internationalbrainlab.org', 
    password='international', silent=True,
    cache_dir = args.base_path
)

freeze_file = 'data/bwm_release.csv'
bwm_df = pd.read_csv(freeze_file, index_col=0)

if args.datasets == "brain-wide-map":
    n_sub = args.n_sessions
    subjects = np.unique(bwm_df.subject)
    selected_subs = np.random.choice(subjects, n_sub, replace=False)
    by_subject = bwm_df.groupby('subject')
    include_eids = np.array([bwm_df.eid[by_subject.groups[sub][0]] for sub in selected_subs])
else:
    with open('data/repro_ephys_release.txt') as file:
        include_eids = [line.rstrip() for line in file]
    include_eids = include_eids[:args.n_sessions]

# Trial setup
params = {
    'interval_len': 2, 'binsize': 0.02, 'single_region': False,

import os
import sys
import argparse
from pathlib import Path
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from one.api import ONE
from datasets import DatasetDict
from utils.ibl_data_utils import (
    prepare_data, 
    select_brain_regions, 
    list_brain_regions, 
    bin_spiking_data,
    bin_behaviors,
    align_spike_behavior
)
from utils.dataset_utils import create_dataset, upload_dataset

ap = argparse.ArgumentParser()
ap.add_argument("--base_path", type=str, default="EXAMPLE_PATH")
ap.add_argument("--datasets", type=str, default="reproducible-ephys", choices=["reproducible-ephys", "brain-wide-map"])
ap.add_argument("--n_sessions", type=int, default=1)
ap.add_argument("--n_workers", type=int, default=1)
args = ap.parse_args()

SEED = 42

np.random.seed(SEED)

one = ONE(
    base_url='https://openalyx.internationalbrainlab.org', 
    password='international', silent=True,
    cache_dir = args.base_path
)

freeze_file = 'data/bwm_release.csv'
bwm_df = pd.read_csv(freeze_file, index_col=0)

if args.datasets == "brain-wide-map":
    n_sub = args.n_sessions
    subjects = np.unique(bwm_df.subject)
    selected_subs = np.random.choice(subjects, n_sub, replace=False)
    by_subject = bwm_df.groupby('subject')
    include_eids = np.array([bwm_df.eid[by_subject.groups[sub][0]] for sub in selected_subs])
else:
    with open('data/repro_ephys_release.txt') as file:
        include_eids = [line.rstrip() for line in file]
    include_eids = include_eids[:args.n_sessions]

    'interval_len': 2, 'binsize': 0.02, 'single_region': False,
    'align_time': 'stimOn_times', 'time_window': (-.5, 1.5)
}

        print(f'Preprocess session {eid}:')

        # Load and preprocess data
        neural_dict, behave_dict, meta_data, trials_data = prepare_data(one, eid, bwm_df, params, n_workers=args.n_workers)
        regions, beryl_reg = list_brain_regions(neural_dict, **params)
        region_cluster_ids = select_brain_regions(neural_dict, beryl_reg, regions, **params)
        binned_spikes, clusters_used_in_bins = bin_spiking_data(
            region_cluster_ids, neural_dict, trials_df=trials_data['trials_df'], n_workers=args.n_workers, **params
        )
        binned_behaviors, behavior_masks = bin_behaviors(
            one, eid, beh_names[3:], trials_df=trials_data['trials_df'], 
            allow_nans=True, n_workers=args.n_workers, **params
        )
        
        # Ensure neural and behavior data match for each trial
        aligned_binned_spikes, aligned_binned_behaviors = align_spike_behavior(
            binned_spikes, binned_behaviors, beh_names, trials_data['trials_mask']
        )

        # Partition dataset (train: 0.7 val: 0.1 test: 0.2)
        max_num_trials = len(aligned_binned_spikes)
        trial_idxs = np.random.choice(np.arange(max_num_trials), max_num_trials, replace=False)
        train_idxs = trial_idxs[:int(0.7*max_num_trials)]
        val_idxs = trial_idxs[int(0.7*max_num_trials):int(0.8*max_num_trials)]
        test_idxs = trial_idxs[int(0.8*max_num_trials):]
    
        train_beh, val_beh, test_beh = {}, {}, {}
        for beh in aligned_binned_behaviors.keys():
            train_beh.update({beh: aligned_binned_behaviors[beh][train_idxs]})
            val_beh.update({beh: aligned_binned_behaviors[beh][val_idxs]})
            test_beh.update({beh: aligned_binned_behaviors[beh][test_idxs]})
        
        train_dataset = create_dataset(
            aligned_binned_spikes[train_idxs], bwm_df, eid, params, 
            binned_behaviors=train_beh, meta_data=meta_data
        )
        val_dataset = create_dataset(
            aligned_binned_spikes[val_idxs], bwm_df, eid, params, 
            binned_behaviors=val_beh, meta_data=meta_data
        )
        test_dataset = create_dataset(
            aligned_binned_spikes[test_idxs], bwm_df, eid, params, 
            binned_behaviors=test_beh, meta_data=meta_data
        )

        # Create dataset
        partitioned_dataset = DatasetDict({
            'train': train_dataset,

        )

        # Cache dataset

        print(f'Cached session {eid}.')
        print(f'Progress: {eid_idx+1} / {len(include_eids)} sessions cached.')
            
    except Exception as e:
        print(f'Skipped session {eid} due to unexpected error: ', e)

2	import os 
3	import sys

5	from tqdm import *
6	import numpy as np
7	import pandas as pd
8	from pathlib import Path
9	import multiprocessing
10	from functools import partial
11	from scipy.interpolate import interp1d
12	from iblutil.numerical import ismember, bincount2D
13	import brainbox.behavior.dlc as dlc
14	from brainbox.io.one import SpikeSortingLoader, SessionLoader
15	from iblatlas.regions import BrainRegions
16	from brainbox.population.decode import get_spike_counts_in_bins
17	
18	
19	def globalize(func):
20	    def result(*args, **kwargs):
21	        return func(*args, **kwargs)
22	    result.__name__ = result.__qualname__ = uuid.uuid4().hex
23	    setattr(sys.modules[result.__module__], result.__name__, result)
24	    return result
25	
26	
27	def load_spiking_data(one, pid, compute_metrics=False, qc=None, **kwargs):
28	    """
29	    Function to load the cluster information and spike trains for clusters that may or may not pass certain quality metrics.
30	
31	    Parameters
32	    ----------
33	    one: one.api.ONE
34	        Instance to be used to connect to local or remote database
35	    pid: str
36	        A probe insertion UUID
37	    compute_metrics: bool
38	        If True, force SpikeSortingLoader.merge_clusters to recompute the cluster metrics. Default is False
39	    qc: float
40	        Quality threshold to be used to select good clusters. Default is None.
41	        If use all available clusters, set qc to None. If use good clusters, set qc to 1.
42	    kwargs:
43	        Keyword arguments passed to SpikeSortingLoader upon initiation. Specifically, if one instance offline,
44	        you need to pass 'eid' and 'pname' here as they cannot be inferred from pid in offline mode.
45	
46	    Returns
47	    -------
48	    selected_spikes: dict
49	        Spike trains associated with clusters. Dictionary with keys ['depths', 'times', 'clusters', 'amps']
50	    selected_clusters: pandas.DataFrame
51	        Information of clusters for this pid 
52	    sampling_freq: float
53	        Sampling frequency of spiking data (action potential)
54	    """
55	    eid = kwargs.pop('eid', '')
56	    pname = kwargs.pop('pname', '')
57	    spike_loader = SpikeSortingLoader(pid=pid, one=one, eid=eid, pname=pname)
58	    sampling_freq = spike_loader.raw_electrophysiology(band="ap", stream=True).fs
59	    
60	    spikes, clusters, channels = spike_loader.load_spike_sorting()
61	    clusters_labeled = SpikeSortingLoader.merge_clusters(
62	        spikes, clusters, channels, compute_metrics=compute_metrics).to_df()
63	    if qc is None:
64	        return spikes, clusters_labeled, sampling_freq
65	    else:
66	        iok = clusters_labeled['label'] >= qc
67	        selected_clusters = clusters_labeled[iok]
68	        spike_idx, ib = ismember(spikes['clusters'], selected_clusters.index)
69	        selected_clusters.reset_index(drop=True, inplace=True)
70	        selected_spikes = {k: v[spike_idx] for k, v in spikes.items()}
71	        selected_spikes['clusters'] = selected_clusters.index[ib].astype(np.int32)

75	def merge_probes(spikes_list, clusters_list):
76	    """
77	    Merge spikes and clusters information from several probes as if they were recorded from the same probe.
78	    This can be used to account for the fact that data from the probes recorded in the same session are not
79	    statistically independent as they have the same underlying behaviour.
80	
81	    NOTE: The clusters dataframe will be re-indexed to avoid duplicated indices. Accordingly, spikes['clusters']
82	    will be updated. To unambiguously identify clusters use the column 'uuids'
83	
84	    Parameters
85	    ----------
86	    spikes_list: list of dicts
87	        List of spike dictionaries as loaded by SpikeSortingLoader or brainwidemap.load_good_units
88	    clusters_list: list of pandas.DataFrames
89	        List of cluster dataframes as loaded by SpikeSortingLoader.merge_clusters or brainwidemap.load_good_units
90	
91	    Returns
92	    -------
93	    merged_spikes: dict
94	        Merged and time-sorted spikes in single dictionary, where 'clusters' is adjusted to index into merged_clusters
95	    merged_clusters: pandas.DataFrame
96	        Merged clusters in single dataframe, re-indexed to avoid duplicate indices.
97	        To unambiguously identify clusters use the column 'uuids'
98	    """
99	
100	    assert (len(clusters_list) == len(spikes_list)), 'clusters_list and spikes_list must have the same length'
101	    assert all([isinstance(s, dict) for s in spikes_list]), 'spikes_list must contain only dictionaries'
102	    assert all([isinstance(c, pd.DataFrame) for c in clusters_list]), 'clusters_list must contain only pd.DataFrames'
103	
104	    merged_spikes = []
105	    merged_clusters = []
106	    cluster_max = 0
107	
108	    for clusters, spikes in zip(clusters_list, spikes_list):
109	        spikes['clusters'] += cluster_max
110	        cluster_max = clusters.index.max() + 1
111	        merged_spikes.append(spikes)
112	        merged_clusters.append(clusters)
113	        
114	    merged_clusters = pd.concat(merged_clusters, ignore_index=True)
115	    merged_spikes = {k: np.concatenate([s[k] for s in merged_spikes]) for k in merged_spikes[0].keys()}
116	    # Sort spikes by spike time
117	    sort_idx = np.argsort(merged_spikes['times'], kind='stable')
118	    merged_spikes = {k: v[sort_idx] for k, v in merged_spikes.items()}
119	
120	    return merged_spikes, merged_clusters

123	def load_trials_and_mask(
124	        one, eid, min_rt=0.08, max_rt=2., nan_exclude='default', min_trial_len=None,
125	        max_trial_len=None, exclude_unbiased=False, exclude_nochoice=True, sess_loader=None):
126	    """
127	    Function to load all trials for a given session and create a mask to exclude all trials that have a reaction time
128	    shorter than min_rt or longer than max_rt or that have NaN for one of the specified events.
129	
130	    Parameters
131	    ----------
132	    one: one.api.ONE
133	        Instance to be used to connect to local or remote database
134	    eid: str
135	        A session UUID
136	    min_rt: float or None
137	        Minimum admissible reaction time in seconds for a trial to be included. Default is 0.08. If None, don't apply.
138	    max_rt: float or None
139	        Maximum admissible reaction time in seconds for a trial to be included. Default is 2. If None, don't apply.
140	    nan_exclude: list or 'default'
141	        List of trial events that cannot be NaN for a trial to be included. If set to 'default' the list is
142	        ['stimOn_times','choice','feedback_times','probabilityLeft','firstMovement_times','feedbackType']
143	    min_trial_len: float or None
144	        Minimum admissible trial length measured by goCue_time (start) and feedback_time (end).
145	        Default is None.
146	    max_trial_len: float or Nona
147	        Maximum admissible trial length measured by goCue_time (start) and feedback_time (end).
148	        Default is None.
149	    exclude_unbiased: bool
150	        True to exclude trials that fall within the unbiased block at the beginning of session.
151	        Default is False.
152	    exclude_nochoice: bool
153	        True to exclude trials where the animal does not respond. Default is False.
154	    sess_loader: brainbox.io.one.SessionLoader or NoneType
155	        Optional SessionLoader object; if None, this object will be created internally
156	
157	    Returns
158	    -------
159	    trials: pandas.DataFrame
160	        Trials table containing all trials for this session. If complete with columns:
161	        ['stimOff_times','goCueTrigger_times','feedbackType','contrastLeft','contrastRight','rewardVolume',
162	        'goCue_times','choice','feedback_times','stimOn_times','response_times','firstMovement_times',
163	        'probabilityLeft', 'intervals_0', 'intervals_1']
164	    mask: pandas.Series
165	        Boolean Series to mask trials table for trials that pass specified criteria. True for all trials that should be
166	        included, False for all trials that should be excluded.
167	    """
168	
169	    if nan_exclude == 'default':
170	        nan_exclude = [
171	            'stimOn_times',
172	            'choice',
173	            'feedback_times',
174	            'probabilityLeft',
175	            'firstMovement_times',
176	            'feedbackType'
177	        ]
178	
179	    if sess_loader is None:
180	        sess_loader = SessionLoader(one, eid)
181	
182	    if sess_loader.trials.empty:
183	        sess_loader.load_trials()
184	
185	    # Create a mask for trials to exclude
186	    # Remove trials that are outside the allowed reaction time range
187	    if min_rt is not None:
188	        query = f'(firstMovement_times - stimOn_times < {min_rt})'
189	    else:
190	        query = ''
191	    if max_rt is not None:
192	        query += f' | (firstMovement_times - stimOn_times > {max_rt})'
193	    # Remove trials that are outside the allowed trial duration range
194	    if min_trial_len is not None:
195	        query += f' | (feedback_times - goCue_times < {min_trial_len})'
196	    if max_trial_len is not None:
197	        query += f' | (feedback_times - goCue_times > {max_trial_len})'
198	    # Remove trials with nan in specified events
199	    for event in nan_exclude:
200	        query += f' | {event}.isnull()'
201	    # Remove trials in unbiased block at beginning
202	    if exclude_unbiased:
203	        query += ' | (probabilityLeft == 0.5)'
204	    # Remove trials where animal does not respond
205	    if exclude_nochoice:
206	        query += ' | (choice == 0)'
207	    # If min_rt was None we have to clean up the string
208	    if min_rt is None:
209	        query = query[3:]
210	
211	    # Create mask
212	    mask = ~sess_loader.trials.eval(query)
213	
214	    return sess_loader.trials, mask

244	def get_spike_data_per_interval(times, clusters, interval_begs, interval_ends, interval_len, binsize, n_workers=os.cpu_count()):
245	    """
246	    Select spiking data for specified interval in each recording.
247	
248	    Parameters
249	    ----------
250	    times : array-like
251	        time in seconds for each spike
252	    clusters : array-like
253	        cluster id for each spike
254	    interval_begs : array-like
255	        beginning of each interval in seconds
256	    interval_ends : array-like
257	        end of each interval in seconds
258	    interval_len : float
259	    binsize : float
260	        width of each bin in seconds
261	
262	    Returns
263	    -------
264	    tuple
265	        - (list): time in seconds for each interval; timepoints refer to the start/left edge of a bin
266	        - (list): data for each interval of shape (n_clusters, n_bins)
267	
268	    """
269	    n_intervals = len(interval_begs)
270	
271	    # np.ceil because we want to make sure our bins contain all data
272	    n_bins = int(np.ceil(interval_len / binsize))
273	
274	    cluster_ids = np.unique(clusters)
275	    n_clusters_in_region = len(cluster_ids)
276	
277	    # This allows multiprocessing to work with nested functions
278	    @globalize
279	    def compute_spike_count(interval):
280	        # We use interval_idx to track the interval order while working with p.imap_unordered()
281	        interval_idx, t_beg, t_end = interval
282	        idxs_t = (times >= t_beg) & (times < t_end)
283	        times_curr = times[idxs_t]
284	        clust_curr = clusters[idxs_t]
285	        if times_curr.shape[0] == 0:
286	            # no spikes in this trial
287	            binned_spikes_tmp = np.zeros((n_clusters_in_region, n_bins))
288	            if np.isnan(t_beg) or np.isnan(t_end):
289	                t_idxs = np.nan * np.ones(n_bins)
290	            else:
291	                t_idxs = np.arange(t_beg, t_end + binsize / 2, binsize)
292	            idxs_tmp = np.arange(n_clusters_in_region)
293	        else:
294	            # bin spikes
295	            binned_spikes_tmp, t_idxs, cluster_idxs = bincount2D(
296	                times_curr, clust_curr, xbin=binsize, xlim=[t_beg, t_end])
297	            # find indices of clusters that returned spikes for this trial
298	            _, idxs_tmp, _ = np.intersect1d(cluster_ids, cluster_idxs, return_indices=True)
299	        return binned_spikes_tmp[:, :n_bins], idxs_tmp, interval_idx
300	
301	    binned_spikes = np.zeros((n_intervals, n_clusters_in_region, n_bins))
302	    with multiprocessing.Pool(processes=n_workers) as p:
303	        intervals = list(zip(np.arange(n_intervals), interval_begs, interval_ends))
304	        with tqdm(total=len(intervals)) as pbar:
305	            for res in p.imap_unordered(compute_spike_count, intervals):
306	                pbar.update()
307	                binned_spikes[res[-1], res[1], :] += res[0]
308	        pbar.close()
309	        p.close()
310	    return binned_spikes

313	def bin_spiking_data(reg_clu_ids, neural_df, intervals=None, trials_df=None, n_workers=os.cpu_count(), **kwargs):
314	    """
315	    Format a single session-wide array of spikes into a list of trial-based arrays.
316	    The ordering of clusters used in the output are also returned.
317	
318	    Parameters
319	    ----------
320	    reg_clu_ids : array-like
321	        array of cluster ids for each spike
322	    neural_df : pd.DataFrame
323	        keys: 'spike_times', 'spike_clusters', 'cluster_regions', 'cluster_qc', 'cluster_df'
324	    intervals : 
325	        array of time intervals for each recording chunk including trials and non-trials
326	    trials_df : pd.DataFrame
327	        columns: 'choice', 'feedback', 'pLeft', 'firstMovement_times', 'stimOn_times',
328	        'feedback_times'
329	    kwargs
330	        align_time : str
331	            event in trial on which to align intervals
332	            'firstMovement_times' | 'stimOn_times' | 'feedback_times'
333	        time_window : tuple
334	            (window_start, window_end), relative to align_time
335	        binsize : float, optional
336	            size of bins in seconds for multi-bin decoding
337	            
338	    Returns
339	    -------
340	    list
341	        each element is a 2D numpy.ndarray for a single interval of shape (n_bins, n_clusters)
342	    array
343	        cluster ids that account for axis 1 of the above 2D arrays.
344	    """
345	
346	    if trials_df is not None:
347	        # compute time intervals for each trial
348	        intervals = np.vstack([
349	            trials_df[kwargs['align_time']] + kwargs['time_window'][0],
350	            trials_df[kwargs['align_time']] + kwargs['time_window'][1]
351	        ]).T
352	        chunk_len = kwargs['time_window'][1] - kwargs['time_window'][0]
353	        interval_len = (
354	            kwargs['time_window'][1] - kwargs['time_window'][0]
355	        )
356	    else:
357	        assert intervals is not None, 'Require intervals to segment the recording into chunks including trials and non-trials.'
358	        chunk_len = intervals[0,1] - intervals[0,0]
359	        interval_len = (
360	            intervals[0,1] - intervals[0,0]
361	        )
362	
363	    # subselect spikes for this region
364	    spikemask = np.isin(neural_df['spike_clusters'], reg_clu_ids)
365	    regspikes = neural_df['spike_times'][spikemask]
366	    regclu = neural_df['spike_clusters'][spikemask]
367	    clusters_used_in_bins = np.unique(regclu)
368	
369	    binsize = kwargs.get('binsize', chunk_len)
370	    
371	    if chunk_len / binsize == 1.0:
372	        # one vector of neural activity per interval
373	        binned, _ = get_spike_counts_in_bins(regspikes, regclu, intervals)
374	        binned = binned.T  # binned is a 2D array
375	        binned_list = [x[None, :] for x in binned]
376	    else:
377	        binned_array = get_spike_data_per_interval(
378	            regspikes, regclu,
379	            interval_begs=intervals[:, 0],
380	            interval_ends=intervals[:, 1],
381	            interval_len=interval_len,
382	            binsize=kwargs['binsize'],
383	            n_workers=n_workers)
384	        binned_list = [x.T for x in binned_array]   
385	    return np.array(binned_list), clusters_used_in_bins

507	def get_behavior_per_interval(
508	    target_times, 
509	    target_vals, 
510	    intervals=None, 
511	    trials_df=None, 
512	    allow_nans=False, 
513	    n_workers=os.cpu_count(), 
514	    **kwargs
515	):
516	    """
517	    Format a single session-wide array of target data into a list of interval-based arrays.
518	
519	    Note: the bin size of the returned data will only be equal to the input `binsize` if that value
520	    evenly divides `align_interval`; for example if `align_interval=(0, 0.2)` and `binsize=0.10`,
521	    then the returned data will have the correct binsize. If `align_interval=(0, 0.2)` and
522	    `binsize=0.06` then the returned data will not have the correct binsize.
523	
524	    Parameters
525	    ----------
526	    target_times : array-like
527	        time in seconds for each sample
528	    target_vals : array-like
529	        data samples
530	    intervals : 
531	        array of time intervals for each recording chunk including trials and non-trials
532	    trials_df : pd.DataFrame
533	        requires a column that matches `align_event`
534	    align_event : str
535	        event to align interval to
536	        firstMovement_times | stimOn_times | feedback_times
537	    align_interval : tuple
538	        (align_begin, align_end); time in seconds relative to align_event
539	    binsize : float
540	        size of individual bins in interval
541	    allow_nans : bool, optional
542	        False to skip intervals with >0 NaN values in target data
543	
544	    Returns
545	    -------
546	    tuple
547	        - (list): time in seconds for each interval
548	        - (list): data for each interval
549	        - (array-like): mask of good intervals (True) and bad intervals (False)
550	
551	    """
552	
553	    binsize = kwargs['binsize']
554	    align_interval = kwargs['time_window']
555	    interval_len = align_interval[1] - align_interval[0]
556	
557	    if trials_df is not None:
558	        align_event = kwargs['align_time']
559	        align_times = trials_df[align_event].values
560	        interval_begs = align_times + align_interval[0]
561	        interval_ends = align_times + align_interval[1]
562	    else:
563	        assert intervals is not None, 'Require intervals to segment the recording into chunks including trials and non-trials.'
564	        interval_begs, interval_ends = intervals.T
565	
566	    n_intervals = len(interval_begs)
567	
568	    if np.all(np.isnan(interval_begs)) or np.all(np.isnan(interval_ends)):
569	        print('interval times all nan')
570	        good_interval = np.nan * np.ones(interval_begs.shape[0])
571	        target_times_list = []
572	        target_vals_list = []
573	        return target_times_list, target_vals_list, good_interval
574	
575	    # np.ceil because we want to make sure our bins contain all data
576	    n_bins = int(np.ceil(interval_len / binsize))
577	
578	    # split data into intervals
579	    idxs_beg = np.searchsorted(target_times, interval_begs, side='right')
580	    idxs_end = np.searchsorted(target_times, interval_ends, side='left')
581	    target_times_og_list = [target_times[ib:ie] for ib, ie in zip(idxs_beg, idxs_end)]
582	    target_vals_og_list = [target_vals[ib:ie] for ib, ie in zip(idxs_beg, idxs_end)]
583	
584	    # interpolate and store
585	    target_times_list = [None for _ in range(len(target_times_og_list))]
586	    target_vals_list = [None for _ in range(len(target_times_og_list))]
587	    good_interval = [None for _ in range(len(target_times_og_list))]
588	    skip_reasons = [None for _ in range(len(target_times_og_list))]
589	
590	    @globalize
591	    def interpolate_behavior(target):
592	        # We use interval_idx to track the interval order while working with p.imap_unordered()
593	        interval_idx, target_time, target_vals = target
594	
595	        is_good_interval, x_interp, y_interp = False, None, None
